title: An easy method for processing and identification of natural and synthetic microfibers and microplastics in indoor and outdoor air
author: Prata, Castro, et al.
materials: To assess the efficiency of the protocol, three spikes were prepared, each containing 3 polystyrene fibers (Polystyrene Standard 2,000,000, Fluka, Chemica) and 3 polyethylene fragments (grounded Polyethylene, Sigma-Aldrich), which were previously kept in 1 % sodium dodecyl sulfate (Sigma-Aldrich) to improve surface tension. These synthetic polymers were preferred to textile fibers, which were difficult to individualize. Spiked samples were then processed similarly to air samples. All particles were recovered except for one polyethylene fragment, translated in an average recovery rate of 94.4 % (Fig. S-1). This missing particle was later found in the inside of the respective NaI beaker, probably by adhering to the glass wall during decantation.

steps.title: Collect airborne particles on filter
steps.instruction: Conduct passive air sampling for 48 h using a 47 mm quartz fiber filter placed in the sampling inlet.

steps.title: Transfer filter to peroxide solution
steps.instruction: Remove the filter, place it in a glass beaker, wash it with distilled water into the beaker, add hydrogen peroxide to reach a final concentration of 15 % (v/v), and incubate at room temperature (~20 °C) for 8 days to digest natural organic matter.

substeps.instruction: Wash the quartz filter with distilled water into a glass beaker.
Add H₂O₂ to obtain a 15 % solution.
Seal the beaker and let stand at ~20 °C for 8 days.

steps.title: Filter peroxide digest
steps.instruction: After the 8‑day incubation, filter the peroxide solution to collect the remaining particles and transfer the retained material to a new container for density separation.

substeps.instruction: Filter the H₂O₂ digest through an appropriate filter (e.g., glass‑fiber filter).
Rinse the filter cake into a clean beaker for the next step.

steps.title: Perform density separation with NaI
steps.instruction: Prepare a saturated NaI solution with a density of 1.6 g cm⁻³, add the retained particles, cover the container, vigorously shake, allow particles to separate, then decant the supernatant while rinsing the beaker walls to recover any adhering fibers.

substeps.instruction: Add the filtered material to the NaI solution and cover the beaker.
Let the mixture stand until separation is complete (fibers/plastics float).
Decant the supernatant, collecting the floating fraction.
Rinse the beaker walls with distilled water to recover any particles stuck to glass.

steps.title: Filter and dry separated particles
steps.instruction: Filter the NaI suspension to collect the floated fibers and plastics onto a filter, rinse the filter with distilled water to remove residual NaI, and dry the filter at ambient conditions before microscopy.

substeps.instruction: Filter the NaI suspension onto a clean filter (e.g., 47 mm quartz filter).
Rinse the filter with distilled water to eliminate NaI residues.
Dry the filter completely (air‑dry or low‑temperature oven).

steps.title: Count and classify fibers
steps.instruction: Examine the dried filter under a stereomicroscope at 6× magnification, photograph the entire 47 mm filter, and manually count and classify each fiber as natural, synthetic, or unknown using the provided classification diagram; record size, colour and origin in ImageJ.

substeps.instruction: Place the dried filter on the stereomicroscope stage.
Observe at 6× magnification and capture images of the whole filter.
Count each fiber and assign it to natural, synthetic or unknown categories according to the diagram.
Measure fibre length and width in ImageJ and note colour and origin.
